title: FRM Operational, Lesson 6: Change risk - most incidents begin with a deployment
subtitle: The system runs for six months and then breaks at two in the morning on a Saturday, right after an update
whyItMatters: Operational risk is usually pictured as fraud and natural disaster, but most real service outages come from inside the organisation: a change that was deployed. This is a risk the firm creates for itself, and for that reason it is also the one most open to control.
openingQuestion: In technology incident statistics at financial institutions, what is the proximate cause of most serious outages?
openingOptions: An external cyber attack against the core infrastructure
A change the organisation pushed into the live system
A hardware failure at the primary data centre site
A fault at a third-party cloud service provider
explanation: A system running stably generally carries on running stably. What breaks that state is usually a change - a patch, a new configuration, a new version, a data migration. This matters because it inverts the intuition about where controls belong: cyber attacks and hardware failures are worth worrying about, but the largest and most predictable window of risk is the moment the organisation puts its own hands on its own systems.

diagram.label: Change requested and classified by impact level
Tested in a production-like environment with realistic data volumes
Deployed in small batches with a checkpoint between each step
A rollback plan that has been tested, not merely written down

realWorldExample.company: A bank migrating its core system
realWorldExample.description: Core system migration failures share a common pattern: testing was thorough on function and thin on volume. Every transaction runs correctly in a test environment holding a few thousand records, and then falls over against a few million real ones on the Monday morning. A rollback plan does exist, but nobody has ever tried running it against data that is already half written.

quiz.question: Why is change risk considered the most controllable category of operational risk?
options: Because its impact is always smaller than that of other incident types
Because the organisation chooses the timing and the scope of the change
Because it only ever affects the information technology systems
Because supervisors have already prescribed a mandatory process for it
quiz.explanation: Unlike a cyber attack or a natural disaster, a change is something the firm does deliberately - it picks when, it picks how much, it picks how long to test first. A risk window known in advance means every control can be placed exactly where it belongs, rather than being a reaction after the event. The impact can be enormous, as any failed core migration shows, and the consequences run straight through to customers rather than staying inside the technology function.

quiz.question: What is the most common weakness of a test environment?
options: It does not use the same programming language as the live system
Not enough staff are involved in testing before the deployment goes ahead
The time allowed for testing is always far shorter than the development time
It is right about function but far off about data volume
quiz.explanation: A few thousand records running correctly says nothing about a few million: database indexes, table lock durations and memory all behave differently at a different scale. This is why so many incidents surface at the first peak hour after a deployment rather than at the moment of deployment itself. The language is normally identical because it is the same codebase, and thin staffing or a compressed schedule are project problems that show up as missed defects of every kind, not as this specific and highly characteristic one.

quiz.question: Why does a rollback plan have to be rehearsed rather than only written?
options: Because written documentation is always longer than there is time to read
Because supervisors require evidence of a quarterly rehearsal
Because the operations staff change over continuously as time passes
Because rolling back once data is partly written is a different problem
quiz.explanation: On paper, rollback means restoring the previous version. In reality the system has been live for three hours and has written data in the new structure - restoring the old state can destroy those transactions. A rollback scenario that has never been tested is almost always longer and riskier than the figure recorded in the document. Staff turnover and document length are real reasons to keep any procedure current, but they apply equally to procedures that work, so neither explains why this one specifically fails.

quiz.question: Why does deploying in small batches with checkpoints reduce risk?
options: Because the blast radius is limited to the batch already deployed
Because the total time taken to deploy is shortened considerably
Because each small batch does not need its own separate testing step
Because it makes a rollback plan unnecessary for the deployment
quiz.explanation: Deploying everything at once means that if it is wrong, it is wrong for every customer. Batching keeps the fault touching only a portion, and the checkpoint between steps gives a chance to stop before going further - at the cost of a longer deployment, which is a price worth paying. Each batch still needs its own verification and the rollback plan matters more rather than less, because the checkpoint is only useful if there is somewhere to go back to.

quiz.question: Why does an emergency change need its own process rather than an exemption from process?
options: Because an emergency change always has a wider scope than a normal one
Because it is the moment of highest risk and least testing time
Because it has to be approved by the board before it can be carried out
Because the cost of an emergency change is always several times higher
quiz.explanation: An emergency change combines the two worst conditions: time pressure and truncated testing. Exempting it from process removes the control at exactly the point it is most needed. The right answer is a shortened but still mandatory process - two-person approval, full logging, and a compulsory review afterwards. Emergency changes are typically narrower rather than wider in scope, board approval would defeat the purpose of speed, and the cost varies with the fault being fixed.

practicePrompt.question: An update to a payment system passes full testing, is deployed on Sunday night, and fails at nine o'clock on Monday morning. What is the most typical cause?
options: The test environment was right on function and wrong on transaction volume
The deployment team skipped a mandatory step in the approval process
Sunday night is the wrong window, so it should move to midweek
The rollback plan had been written but nobody had ever read it again
practicePrompt.explanation: A test environment is almost always several orders of magnitude smaller than production in volume, so it proves the software does the RIGHT THING without proving it can carry the LOAD. Faults of this class - resource locks, queues overflowing, queries degrading - only appear once real traffic arrives, which means the first peak hour after deployment. It is also why deploying in small batches with checkpoints beats one large cutover: it puts a slice of real traffic through early, while the rollback scope is still small and there is still time.

keyTakeaways: Most serious service outages originate in a change the organisation deployed itself
This is the most controllable operational risk, because the timing and the scope are both chosen
Test environments tend to be right on function and wrong on volume - so incidents surface at the first peak hour
An emergency change needs a shortened process rather than an exemption, because it is the moment of highest risk

summary.keyIdea: Change risk is the risk an organisation creates for itself, and that is the good news: the risk window is known in advance, so controls can be placed exactly where they belong instead of reacting after the fact.

application.message: After every technology incident, the first question should be whether any change was deployed in the preceding 72 hours. The answer is yes most of the time, and it shortens the search for the cause considerably.

sections.text: A system that has run smoothly for six months rarely breaks on its own. It breaks after somebody touched it - and that is the single most useful fact in all of technology risk management.
A self-inflicted risk is a risk known in advance

A cyber attack arrives when the attacker chooses. A natural disaster arrives when it arrives. But a change is something the organisation schedules itself, scopes itself, and tests for as long as it decides. The risk window sits entirely within its control, which makes change both the largest source of incidents and the highest-return place to invest in controls.

A test environment is usually right on function: every business flow that runs through it produces the correct result. What it rarely matches is volume. A few thousand records and a few million records are two different problems for database indexes, for table lock duration, and for memory. That is why incidents tend to detonate at the first busy trading session rather than at the moment the deploy button is pressed.
Rollback is a scenario, not a button

In the documentation, rollback means restoring the previous version. In practice the system has been live for several hours and has written data in the new structure. Restoring the old state can erase those transactions, while keeping them leaves data the old version cannot read. A rollback plan that has never been rehearsed is always more optimistic than reality.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: An emergency change combines time pressure with truncated testing - the two worst conditions at once. Exempting it from process removes the control at exactly the point it is most needed.
